executive_summary: NZD/JPY sits at 91.638, the close of the gated weekday store on 3 September 2026, two sessions after the 1 September valuation date and one session after the RBNZ decision. The pair has fallen 1.35 per cent over one month, 1.52 per cent over three and 2.59 per cent over six, while remaining 4.54 per cent higher over twelve — a carry cross that earned its keep for a year and has just given back two months of gains in two sessions, dropping 2.74 yen (2.90 per cent) from 94.380 on 1 September to 91.638 on 3 September. The dominant bilateral narrative is a policy-path inversion that neither standalone dossier captures: the RBNZ delivered a second consecutive 25bp hike to 2.75 per cent on 2 September but published a track implying gradualism, while the Bank of Japan has moved from faster than market expectations in print to board members publicly floating a larger-than-usual move on 18 September. Faster BoJ normalisation risk means a stronger yen and slower-than-hoped RBNZ tightening means a weaker Kiwi, and that alignment explains why NZD/JPY moved more aggressively than either central-bank headline implies in isolation. Three bilateral facts diverge sharply from the standalone views: the base dossier's principal tactical edge resolved against it; the quote dossier's central puzzle, a yen that would not rally on narrowing spreads, has just been resolved in the yen's favour; and the 150bp policy differential that funds this cross (175bp post-hike) narrows on almost every plausible path from here as the BoJ delivers 50-75bp of consensus tightening against an RBNZ with roughly one move left. The settled direction is Bearish at both horizons, conviction 3, tactical score -0.1885 and strategic score -0.3393 — and the caveat is not the direction but the entry: the pair is sitting 39 pips above the heaviest support band on its own chart after a three-sigma two-day move, so the thesis is right and the price has partly caught up with it.

market_context.valuation_assessment: There is no usable pair-level fair value here. On the BIS real effective basis NZD sits at 101.12 (June 2026) against JPY at 65.30, a 54.9 per cent relative real gap implying an NZD/JPY REER parity near 42.7 — a number both dossiers explicitly label an artefact of the yen's index base and economically meaningless. What the REER comparison establishes is direction without timing: the yen is the cheapest major currency in the world on a real effective basis, 30.4 points below the next-cheapest currency and 8.73 points cheaper over the year to June, while the New Zealand dollar sits almost exactly on its own index base. Structural valuation is therefore one-sided in the yen's favour across the entire horizon and has been for three years without once being a timing signal. At the 62nd closing percentile of a 52-week range only 9.90 yen wide (roughly 10.8 per cent of spot), the pair is priced neither for a carry regime break nor for a continuation of the 2025-26 grind higher.

market_context.recent_regime: The regime broke in the first week of September after five months of range. From the 3 August post-intervention trough of 91.572 the pair rallied almost without interruption to 95.17455 on 25 August, then stalled for six sessions as the 25 August high failed to clear the May peak. On 2 September the RBNZ raised the OCR to 2.75% and the pair fell 1.51 yen; on 3 September it fell a further 1.23 yen, touching 91.271. The pair fell more than 1% despite a second consecutive hike because markets traded the future path rather than the decision, with a 4-2 committee split and a dovish OCR track, while the yen was the strongest major on a combined risk-aversion carry unwind and an independently more hawkish BoJ story. Three yen-positive impulses that failed all year — record intervention, a 30-year high in JGB yields, and a narrowing spread — have finally been joined by a fourth, a repriced policy path, and this time the cross has responded.

bilateral_carry_analysis.carry_assessment: The annualised carry for a long NZD/JPY position is 150bp on the payload's rates block, widening to 175bp after the 2 September RBNZ hike. The futures-implied roll premium is -192.7bp annualised (6J/6N calendar spread, observed 2026-08-31), exceeding the 175bp policy differential by roughly 18bp — a persistent funding tax attributable to cross-currency basis. Carry has worked in this cross and only in this cross for the base currency over the trailing year (+7.49%), but it is working less well now: retail carry strategies leveraged against weak yen levels paid off handsomely in H1 2026, but research houses caution that surprise yen-buying intervention could drag NZD/JPY lower in sympathy, and the complex has been diversifying its funding leg away from the yen toward the Swiss franc, meaning the unwind when it comes is concentrated in the crosses that still use yen as funding. On any measure — 0.195 on the payload's own estimate, 0.165-0.181 corrected, or 0.158-0.184 against current realised vol — this is a mediocre risk-adjusted carry, and a move to a 13-15% volatility regime that accompanies a carry unwind takes the ratio to roughly 0.12-0.13 without either central bank doing anything.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The bilateral policy differential is +150bp in the New Zealand dollar's favour (OCR 2.50% against a BoJ target of around 1.00% in the gated rates block), and the RBNZ has since taken the OCR to 2.75% on 2 September, widening it to 175bp on the day. The trajectory, however, has turned against the pair. The RBNZ's republished OCR track indicated only the chance of one further quarter-point move before year-end, and local commentary characterised the statement as more dovish than anticipated against a market that had been positioned for a published peak nearer 3.5%; the hawkish guidance gap the base dossier identified as its principal tactical edge therefore closed to the downside rather than the upside. On the other leg, the 18 September Bank of Japan meeting sits squarely inside the tactical window with roughly 80-90% of a 25bp move to 1.25% priced, and cumulative pricing implies only about 1.21% by the 18 December decision against an economist terminal distribution now centred on 1.75%. The transmission is direct: NZD/JPY is a carry cross whose spot level is a levered function of the front-end spread, and the residual repricing risk inside four weeks is concentrated on the Japanese leg because the New Zealand event has already resolved without a hawkish surprise. Carry accrual over four weeks is roughly 12-15bp, trivial against a 3-month ATM implied volatility of 7.69% and provides no cushion.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the differential compresses on almost every plausible path and that is the core strategic argument against the pair. From 175bp post-2 September, the RBNZ's own track allows for roughly one further 25bp move to 3.00%, with the base dossier's own strategic view being that the cycle stops there and that the 9 December Monetary Policy Statement revises the track down. The Bank of Japan, by contrast, is expected to reach 1.25% on 18 September and consensus has 35 of 54 economists at 1.50% or higher by end-March 2027, with half of a separate panel naming 1.75% as terminal. On those paths the differential narrows from 175bp toward 125bp by the 18 December BoJ meeting and toward 100-125bp thereafter, a 50 to 75bp compression in the single input that has driven this cross for a year. The term-structure leg points the same way: the 10-year gap of 179bp is already eroding from the Japanese side as the JGB 10-year prints 3.00% for the first time since 1996, while New Zealand's 4.74% is anchored by a small twin-deficit borrower's term premium. The offsetting consideration is that part of the JGB yield rise is a fiscal risk premium with no currency-positive content, scored separately in Factor 8, which partially neutralises the mechanical read of the spread.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The inflation differential is large in level and pointing the wrong way in composition. New Zealand headline CPI is 4.1% against Japanese headline of 1.9%, a 220bp gap, but the New Zealand overshoot is imported: tradables are 4.9% on a 27.5% petrol contribution, the RBNZ's sectoral factor model core has been pinned at 2.7% for four consecutive quarters, and the RBNZ itself noted that excluding vehicle fuels annual inflation was 2.9%, inside the band. Japan's is the opposite shape: headline 1.9% and core 1.8% understate a BoJ ex-special-factors measure of 2.3% that has been at or above target for twenty-two months, with Tokyo core accelerating three months running and a government energy subsidy suppressing the printed figure by roughly 40-50bp. Growth momentum also favours the quote currency: Japanese unemployment is 2.4% against New Zealand's decade-high 5.6%, the June Tankan printed +22 for large manufacturers and +37 for large non-manufacturers, while New Zealand retail volumes fell 0.5% in the June quarter and house prices sit roughly 17% below their 2021 peak. The two economies collide directly on 17 September, when the New Zealand Q2 GDP release and the Japanese August national CPI print land on the same day. Confidence is capped at 52 because New Zealand survey data is genuinely firm, with ANZ past activity jumping 6.7 points to 16.4 and pricing intentions at 51.0, which skews the GDP risk to the upside of the 0.8% run rate.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the composition asymmetry becomes decisive. New Zealand's overshoot mechanically unwinds: Brent has fallen roughly 12% from its July high, the RBNZ's own track has CPI at 2.4% by mid-2027 and 2.0% by September 2027, one-year inflation expectations collapsed 81bp to 2.60% in the August survey, and there is no wage-price mechanism available with real wages falling 2.1% into a 5.6% unemployment rate. Japan's inflation is going the other way: the energy-subsidy suppression unwinds mechanically over the same window, the BoJ expects core clearly above 2% from H2 FY2026, FY2027 core CPI was revised UP to 2.4% in the July Outlook, and the third consecutive shunto above 5% has produced the longest run of nominal earnings above 3% in 34 years. The two inflation paths cross inside the strategic horizon, and with them the policy paths. Growth reinforces it: New Zealand's survey-versus-hard-data wedge historically resolves toward the hard data, while Japan's Q2 miss was largely a strategic-oil-reserve inventory effect with capex up 1.6% y/y against a 0.2% consensus. The bearish read is capped only by the narrowness of Japanese price increases and the queued rice disinflation.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the clearest bullish factor for the pair and the reason a Bearish net stance is held with conviction 3 rather than higher. NZD/JPY is the purest risk barometer in G10 FX after AUD/JPY, combining the highest-beta risk-on leg with the deepest funding leg, and the current cross-asset configuration is close to as carry-friendly as it gets. VIX closed at 14.43-14.51 in late August against 20.66 a month earlier, a fall of more than six points; US IG OAS is 79bp and HY 263bp, both near cycle tights; the S&P 500 finished August at 7,686 and the Nikkei 225 at 66,129, up 58.4% over twelve months. The Fed Chair has publicly described credit spreads as near the low ends of their historical ranges. In a regime like this the funding currency bleeds and the high-beta currency is carried, which is precisely the mechanism through which the base dossier records New Zealand dollar carry having worked in exactly one place. The bilateral qualification is that the base leg has conspicuously failed to monetise this backdrop against the dollar, gaining only 0.48% in a month in which the broad dollar index fell 2.04 points — so the pair's risk beta is currently being delivered almost entirely by yen weakness rather than New Zealand dollar strength, which makes it hostage to the yen leg.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the same configuration inverts, because a VIX of 14.4 and a high-yield spread of 263bp are levels to fade rather than extrapolate, and NZD/JPY has the worst convexity in the G10 to that fade. The modal path remains continuation, which is why confidence is only 52, but the distribution is heavily skewed: the base currency has the lowest liquidity in the G10, no standing Fed dollar swap line, a current account deficit of 3.6% of GDP requiring continuous foreign funding and an NIIP of minus 42.8% of GDP, while the quote currency is the instrument every carry unwind is settled into. Identified triggers are dated and specific: a Fed hiking into a labour market that printed minus 23,000 payrolls in July with 103,000 of downward revisions, a US appropriations deadline on 30 September, US midterms on 3 November, and an unresolved Strait of Hormuz situation. The August 2024 analogue is the relevant template, and the mechanism is arithmetic: at 7.7% implied volatility the carry-to-vol ratio is 0.195, and a move to a 13-15% regime takes it to roughly 0.10-0.12, at which point the position is unattractive on a risk-adjusted basis without any change in either policy rate.

factors.horizon_split: The stance flips from Bullish to Bearish across horizons purely on where the risk indicators sit in their distributions. Over four weeks a VIX of 14.4 and HY spread of 263bp are simply prevailing conditions and subsidise a carry cross every day they persist. Over six months those same readings are extremes from which the distribution of outcomes is heavily skewed to deterioration, and NZD/JPY is the G10 cross with the worst convexity to that deterioration. Report note, not a re-score: the price payload and subsequent research corroborate the strategic stance faster than the tactical one anticipated — the yen carry unwind is showing up on the tape, and the 2024 analogue moved the relevant implied correlation from +0.6 to -0.9 in about eight weeks, the same window AUD/JPY fell from 109 to 90. tactical.bilateral_analysis: Speculative positioning is short both legs, which mutes the pair signal almost exactly. CFTC leveraged funds were net short 31,994 NZD contracts (36% of 88,964 open interest) and net short 77,042 JPY contracts (20% of 384,216 open interest). The New Zealand dollar short is proportionally larger, which on its own would argue for a bullish squeeze asymmetry. Working against that is the pair-specific flow CFTC data does not capture: Japanese retail margin accounts were net long foreign currency by JPY 4,126bn at end-July at a 2.05:1 ratio, and NZD/JPY is a core holding of that book precisely because it carries the widest liquid carry the New Zealand dollar earns. That is a crowded long in the pair itself, held by leveraged retail, sitting on top of two offsetting professional shorts in the legs. The July intervention episode forced 41,165 contracts of yen covering in a single week, demonstrating how fast the yen leg can gap. Positioning generates no directional signal over four weeks.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the futures books turn over too fast to matter, but two structural flows survive the horizon and both are bearish for the pair. The first is Japanese life-insurer hedge ratios, which sit at historically low levels, with the explicit consequence that normalising them would prompt corresponding yen purchases as hedge costs fall. The second is GPIF, which ended the June quarter with foreign equities at 25.33% against a 25% policy target, mechanically implying multi-trillion-yen foreign-asset sales to rebalance. Against those, the base leg offers no equivalent structural bid: there is no meaningful NZD ETF, no reserve-manager demand of consequence, and a futures market so small that any sustained directional flow moves spot rather than open interest. The pair-level risk is that BoJ normalisation erodes the 150bp carry that funds the Japanese retail NZD/JPY book.

tactical.unwind_trigger: A Bank of Japan hike on 18 September delivered with explicit acceleration language, repeating the Summary of Opinions formulation that the pace will be faster than market expectations, would reprice the December implied rate from 1.21% toward 1.46% and hit the Japanese retail NZD/JPY carry book directly, since that book is funded at the policy rate and is long the pair.
tactical.historical_analogue: The 31 July 2026 joint Japan-US intervention forced 41,165 contracts of yen covering in a single week and moved USD/JPY roughly nine big figures, dragging every cross-yen pair with it. The August 2024 carry unwind is the deeper analogue: NZD/JPY and AUD/JPY were the epicentre because the crowded position was in the crosses rather than in the dollar pair.
tactical.contrarian_case: The case against our own Neutral is that both professional shorts are unremarkable while the crowded position is a leveraged retail long in the pair itself, held at 2.05:1 by accounts that add on strength and liquidate on gaps. In a cross with this little depth, a retail book unwinding is a faster and more disorderly mechanism than any CFTC-visible squeeze, and it is invisible in the data everyone watches. That is precisely what the tape has begun to show since the payload's spot date.

strategic.combined_positioning_signal: On a one-to-six month view the contrarian case is mildly bearish the pair. The visible speculative shorts in both legs will have turned over several times inside six months and carry no information. What survives is a one-directional structural yen bid from life-insurer hedge-ratio normalisation and GPIF rebalancing, against a base currency with no ETF, no reserve-manager demand and the second-smallest futures market in the G10.
strategic.unwind_trigger: Japanese life insurers raising hedge ratios from historic lows as hedging costs fall with a rising BoJ policy rate, combined with the 18 December BoJ decision taking the policy rate to a level at which the NZD/JPY carry no longer covers the volatility. Both are consequences of the base-case rate path rather than shocks, which is what makes them dangerous.
strategic.historical_analogue: Every prior BoJ normalisation step has been accompanied by a reduction in the Japanese retail cross-yen carry book, and the base dossier names Japanese retail margin accounts explicitly as a significant unmeasured holder of NZD/JPY exposure. The 2024 episode showed the sequence: the carry cross moves first and furthest, the dollar pair follows.
strategic.contrarian_case: Hedge-ratio normalisation has been forecast for three years and has not happened, none of the ten surveyed insurers plans to increase unhedged foreign bonds but nor have they said when they will hedge existing ones, and the timing of a structural flow with no trigger date is genuinely unknowable. A thesis whose mechanism has no schedule can be right and unprofitable for a very long time.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the factor where the two dossiers cancel most precisely, and a Neutral here is a considered conclusion. Both economies are being hit by the same energy shock from opposite ends of an identical commodity complex. New Zealand's July merchandise trade balance was minus NZD 1.95bn against an expectation nearer minus NZD 175mn, and the ANZ World Commodity Price Index fell 3.9% in July with the dairy sub-index down 6.5% on the month and 11.3% on the year. Japan's July trade balance was a deficit of JPY 638.3bn against JPY 156.3bn a year earlier, a 4.1-fold widening, with mineral fuels at 22.1% of all imports and up 53.5% y/y on falling volumes. Both dossiers score their own external factor as Bearish at 58 confidence tactically, and the netting is therefore essentially exact. The bilateral trade relationship itself is immaterial to the cross: IMF DOTS shows a net goods balance of minus USD 0.4bn, a rounding error against either country's total external accounts.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.16 strategic weight this is the second-heaviest factor in the model and it contributes nothing, which is itself the most important thing to say about it. The level comparison is a large and durable yen positive: Japan runs a current account surplus of roughly 4.7-5.0% of GDP and a positive NIIP of JPY 560trn, while New Zealand runs a deficit of 3.6% of GDP and an NIIP of minus 42.8%. The trajectory comparison points the other way with roughly equal force: Japan's terms of trade fell 9.8% in two quarters against New Zealand's 2.0% in one, Japan produced its first monthly current-account deficit in seventeen months in June, and its surplus is 27.6 times more primary income than goods, generating far less spot yen demand than its headline implies. Both dossiers independently score their own external factor as the heaviest strategic bearish contributor at almost identical confidence — New Zealand 62, Japan 64 — so the bilateral netting is marginally in the yen's favour and well inside the noise. The commodity direction rules produce the one genuine tilt, modestly bullish for the pair, which pulls an otherwise level-driven Bearish read back to Neutral.

factors.horizon_split: Neutral at both horizons with confidence falling only two points, from 52 to 50, as the weight rises from 0.06 to 0.16. The offset is structural rather than coincidental: New Zealand and Japan are being hit by the same energy and commodity complex from opposite sides of the same trade. What changes with the horizon is only that the stock-level gap becomes more visible relative to the flow deterioration.

net_commodity_exposure.base_commodity_profile: New Zealand is a soft-commodity exporter and a net energy importer. Dairy is roughly 30% of merchandise exports, the ANZ dairy sub-index is down 11.3% y/y, and Fonterra cut its 2026/27 farmgate forecast from a NZD 9.75 to a NZD 9.25 midpoint on 13 July. Petrol and diesel are imported (27.5% petrol contribution to the 4.1% CPI print). Net: dairy up is strongly positive, oil up is mildly negative.
net_commodity_exposure.quote_commodity_profile: Japan imports essentially all of its hydrocarbons. Mineral fuels were 22.1% of July imports and rose 53.5% y/y on volumes that fell — crude value +87.8% on volume +5.5%, LNG value +22.5% on volume -4.8%, JKM LNG roughly doubled y/y at USD 22.71/mmbtu. Net: oil up is strongly negative, LNG up is very strongly negative, with no offsetting commodity export.
net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Using the framework's direction rules: oil up is -- for JPY as a total energy importer against a mild - for NZD, whose export basket is unaffected — net effect the pair RISES, bullish NZD/JPY. LNG (JKM) up is -- for JPY explicitly with no NZD leg — net effect the pair RISES, and at +101.9% y/y JKM is the single largest live commodity input in this cross. Dairy up is ++ for NZD with no JPY leg, so four consecutive positive GDT auctions are mildly bullish for the pair, but with WMP still below its 2 June level and the ANZ dairy sub-index down 11.3% y/y the dairy leg is currently a small negative. Summing: energy up is a clear net positive for the pair because the quote currency's exposure is total and the base currency's partial, while dairy weakness is a smaller net negative affecting only the base leg. The commodity channel alone is therefore modestly bullish NZD/JPY, which is what holds this factor at Neutral rather than letting the current-account level differential drive it Bearish.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Japan's monthly mineral fuel bill rises by roughly JPY 270bn on current volumes, pushing the terms-of-trade index below 79 and making consecutive monthly current-account deficits the base case; New Zealand's tradables inflation is sustained, supporting the OCR path but worsening its own terms of trade. Net: the pair rises roughly 0.8 to 1.5%, with the caveat that a Hormuz-driven spike carries a simultaneous risk-off impulse hitting the base leg harder through Factor 3, which can reverse the sign.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Japan's terms of trade recover toward 86 and its current account returns to comfortable surplus, while New Zealand's petrol base effect unwinds faster, taking headline CPI toward 3% by the October print and ending the RBNZ cycle at 3.00%. Net: the pair falls roughly 1.0 to 2.0%, because the disinflationary hit to the base leg's policy path outweighs the trade-channel gain to the quote leg.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Crude oil and JKM LNG, acting through the Japanese import bill rather than the New Zealand export basket, because Japan's energy exposure is total and running at +53.5% y/y while dairy has at least stopped falling.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The guidance divergence has resolved against the pair. The RBNZ is the only G10 central bank that publishes its own projected policy path, making the 2 September Monetary Policy Statement the highest-information guidance event in the G10 calendar — and it did not deliver the hawkish surprise the base dossier was positioned for. The Committee raised the OCR unanimously to 2.75% but the republished track indicated only the chance of one further quarter-point move before year-end, characterised locally as more dovish than anticipated against a market debating a published peak of 3.28-3.50%. The Bank of Japan's guidance runs the other way and is still unresolved: the 10 August Summary of Opinions contains formulations that the pace of hikes will be faster than market expectations, Takata dissented in July for an immediate move to 1.25%, Deputy Governor Himino called on 27 August for raising rates in a timely manner and warned a weak yen could push up inflation faster than in the past, and the US Treasury Secretary said at the G20 on 31 August that he expects the BoJ to act in ways that lead to a stronger yen. Reporting into the 18 September meeting suggests the Board favours a 25bp hike with a flexible future pace, marginally softer than the Summary of Opinions language but still leaving the December implied rate of 1.21% looking under-priced.

tactical.what_is_priced: The RBNZ's guidance gap has closed and is now priced; the BoJ's has not, with December pricing implying one hike and nothing more against a Board that has said in writing it intends to move faster than the market expects.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: The strategic guidance divergence is the cleanest calendar-anchored bearish argument for the pair, because both banks publish projections inside the window and are expected to move in opposite directions. The RBNZ republishes its OCR track on 9 December, and the base dossier's strategic view is that this is where a downward revision lands: the petrol base effect unwinds in October, September-quarter labour data on 4 November should show unemployment above 5.6%, and a Bank whose May track was already wrong within six weeks has demonstrated it revises. The BoJ publishes its Outlook Report on 30 October, two days after the RBNZ's Monetary Policy Review on 28 October; the July edition had already revised FY2027 core CPI UP to 2.4% while reframing the objective toward preventing an upward deviation — a reaction-function change that converts every upside surprise into a tightening impulse. The Board also abolished the interim assessment of its bond-purchase plan, raising the probability of an unscheduled hawkish move. On credibility the comparison is less lopsided, which is why confidence is 60 rather than higher.

factors.horizon_split: Bearish at both horizons with confidence rising from 56 to 60 as the weight nearly doubles from 0.07 to 0.12. Tactically the RBNZ event has already resolved and only the BoJ's 18 September press-conference language remains live. Strategically both banks publish projection rounds inside the window and the expected direction of each revision is opposite, so the divergence compounds. Report note, not a re-score: Takata has called 2026 a regime change with rate hikes becoming nimble and data-dependent, with markets now pricing over 90% odds of a September hike; the 56/60 confidences stand as issued but the surprise risk has narrowed further onto the bearish side.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The tactical event distribution is asymmetric against the pair for one dominant reason: official yen-buying intervention only ever operates in one direction, and it drags every cross-yen pair with it. The Ministry of Finance has spent roughly JPY 27.1trn buying yen in calendar 2026 against a previous full-year record of JPY 15.32trn, including JPY 15,399.3bn between 30 July and 26 August and a joint operation with the US Treasury on 31 July. Finance Minister Katayama has said Japan will not hesitate to conduct further joint intervention and plans to use the Fed's FIMA repo facility. There is no corresponding official seller of yen and no official participant with any interest in supporting the New Zealand dollar. On the base leg the tactical calendar is comparatively benign, with the PREFU on 29 September sitting at the very edge of the window. The genuinely ambiguous input is the Strait of Hormuz — higher oil is a strong yen negative through the import bill but simultaneously a risk-off impulse that hits the highest-beta cross harder. Confidence is 53 because intervention has a demonstrated half-life of under a month.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the political calendar is materially more hostile to the base leg than to the quote leg, and the geopolitical tail is hostile to the pair on both channels. New Zealand runs a three-year parliamentary cycle with a general election expected in November 2026, preceded by the PREFU on 29 September, into a sovereign carrying negative outlooks from two of three rating agencies. Japan by contrast has an LDP-Ishin supermajority won in February 2026 and no scheduled national election inside the horizon. For a pure risk-proxy cross, almost every identifiable geopolitical tail resolves bearish: Hormuz escalation, a China demand shock, a US midterm surprise, or a US appropriations failure all produce risk-off, and the yen is the currency every one is settled into. The counterweight is that an oil-driven escalation is genuinely two-sided because it damages Japan's external accounts directly and continuously.

factors.horizon_split: Bearish at both horizons with confidence essentially unchanged, 53 tactically and 52 strategically, but for different reasons. Tactically the driver is the one-directional official yen bid. Strategically the intervention option persists but its half-life is under a month, replaced as the dominant channel by New Zealand's election-and-fiscal-update cluster and by the observation that for a pure risk-proxy cross almost every geopolitical tail resolves the same direction.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: This is the one factor where the level comparison and the live repricing both favour the base currency, and it is the principal bullish offset to the rate view. New Zealand's fiscal position is conservative and currently running ahead of plan: net core Crown debt was 41.3% of GDP, NZD 2.8bn better than the Budget forecast, with S&P at AA+ foreign currency and AAA local currency, stable outlook. Japan's is the opposite: general government gross debt roughly 214.5% of GDP, FY2027 budget requests approximately JPY 143trn, and a record JPY 36.6trn debt-servicing line because the Ministry raised its assumed interest rate to 3.8% from 3.0%. The JGB market is repricing this in real time — the 10-year touched 3.00% on 1 September for the first time since 1996, the 2-year hit a 31-year high, and 25s30s is inverted. A rise in JGB yields driven by fiscal risk premium carries no yen-positive content, so it does not narrow the pair's effective differential and is a live yen negative.

tactical.what_is_priced: The JGB market has priced Japan's fiscal deterioration and the FX market has not priced its consequence; New Zealand's negative outlooks are priced nowhere observable.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the fiscal channel remains a net positive for the pair but the margin narrows, because New Zealand's own risks crystallise inside the window while Japan's are partially backstopped. Each further 100bp of BoJ tightening costs roughly JPY 5trn of debt service, ~0.9% of GDP annually, at exactly the moment the Bank is reducing its own JGB purchases — supply rising as the dominant buyer withdraws. The FY2027 draft budget Cabinet approval in late December decides whether the fiscal channel or the policy channel dominates the yen into 2027. Against that, roughly 90% of JGBs are domestically held and all three agencies carry Japan on stable outlook, a genuine backstop. On the New Zealand side, net core Crown debt rises from 41.9% of GDP FY25 to a peak of 46.1% in FY28, and the PREFU published into an election campaign is the natural venue for that to be marked to market. Both sovereigns are deteriorating; Japan's is larger, faster and actively repricing.

strategic.what_is_priced: Sovereign risk is priced at essentially zero for New Zealand and at a visible term premium for Japan in the JGB curve but not in the yen; the FX market has not resolved which mispricing closes first.

factors.horizon_split: Bullish at both horizons with confidence slipping one point from 54 to 53. Tactically Japan's fiscal channel is the active one while New Zealand has nothing scheduled inside four weeks. Strategically New Zealand's PREFU, election and two negative outlooks all land inside the window and narrow the gap, even as Japan's debt-service arithmetic compounds with each BoJ hike.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The volatility landscape generates no directional signal but it does say something important about cost. The gated store carries an NZD/JPY ATM implied volatility term structure of 7.34% at 38.6 days, 7.692% at 94.7 days and 7.91% at 185.7 days — orderly contango with no event kink despite a window containing an FOMC, a BoJ decision, a Japanese CPI print and a New Zealand GDP release. Against 60-day realised of roughly 7.25%, the near-dated implied carries a premium of only about 0.1 to 0.45 volatility points, close to nothing for that event density. Two caveats attach: the payload states this vol is an estimate built from the variance identity with a realised correlation of 0.533 standing in for an unobservable implied one, understating direct quotes by 8.7 to 17.8% in tested cases and a 14.4% median across seventeen pairs, so true 3-month ATM is plausibly 8.3-9.1%; and no 25-delta risk reversal for this cross is obtainable from any free source, so the closest read is that USD/JPY one-month 25-delta sits at -1.74, implying NZD/JPY downside strikes are almost certainly rich.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the structural read is unavailable by design and the volatility read is genuinely neutral, so a Neutral at low confidence is the honest answer. This pass is deliberately not given trailing returns, moving averages, support and resistance zones or the daily OHLC series. What can be said from the supplied vol data is that the term structure from 38.6 to 185.7 days rises only 0.57 volatility points, ordinary slope carrying no premium for a New Zealand general election, a Japanese FY2027 budget approval, US midterms or two projection rounds. On an absolute basis 7.91% six-month implied is not expensive for a cross combining the G10's least liquid currency with its principal funding currency, and if the payload's documented understatement is corrected the true level is nearer 8.6-9.3%, still unremarkable. Liquidity is the structurally important observation: NZD/JPY is a thin cross, spreads widen materially outside Australasian and Tokyo hours, Japanese retail margin platforms are a significant share of turnover, and the pair gaps.

factors.horizon_split: Neutral at both horizons with confidence falling from 50 to 48. The vol landscape is identical in shape at both, and neither horizon produces a directional signal, but strategic confidence is lower because the single input available carries less information over six months than over four weeks, and because no skew instrument exists to corroborate it at any tenor. Second-pass structural completion (not a re-score): spot 91.638 has broken below the 50-day (93.672), 100-day (93.498) and 200-day (92.724) while the stack remains bullishly ordered, and the pair sits 267 pips above a rising 200-week average at 88.968 it has never closed below in this cycle. 20-day realised is now 9.52% against a 60-day of 8.40% and estimated 3-month implied of 7.692%, so realised now exceeds even the corrected implied floor.

expression_assessment.vol_landscape_summary: 20-day realised of 9.52% now sits above the estimated 6-month implied of 7.91%, so long vega is cheap on any basis; but with no quotable NZD/JPY surface and no skew, an options expression in this cross is priced by a single dealer rather than a market.
expression_assessment.directional_expression: The volatility landscape argues for expressing the bearish view primarily through spot or forwards rather than options, and the reason is skew rather than the ATM level. There is no NZD/JPY risk reversal quote, but USD/JPY one-month 25-delta sits at -1.74 volatility points and EUR/JPY at -1.84, so yen-upside strikes are richly bid across the complex and NZD/JPY downside strikes will inherit that premium — paying up for the specific strikes that express the view is expensive in a cross whose ATM is itself an understated estimate. Against that, the short pays away only 192.7bp annualised on the rolled futures basis, a third less than the equivalent USD/JPY expression and comfortably inside target magnitudes. The execution cost of dealer discretion in an options expression is likely to exceed the theoretical vega edge.
expression_assessment.event_timing_consideration: The tactical distribution is concentrated in the 16-18 September cluster (FOMC on the 16th, simultaneous New Zealand Q2 GDP and Japanese August CPI on the 17th, BoJ on the 18th), with a second, tighter collision on 28-30 October (RBNZ Review then BoJ Outlook) and the decisive strategic date on 9 December (RBNZ track republication) followed by the BoJ on the 18th.
expression_assessment.liquidity_note: This is a thin cross with turnover concentrated in Australasian and Tokyo hours; yen crosses are prone to sharp, gapping moves around BoJ meetings and intervention-related headlines, so slippage and gap assumptions must be worse than for a G10 major and stops should be set on a closing rather than an intraday basis.

factors.weight_adjustment_reason: Reduced from defaults of 0.11 and 0.12. NZD/JPY carries no dollar leg, so the factor operates only through the vehicle-currency channel and through the dollar smile's differential effect on a high-beta currency versus a funding currency — both real but second-order. The freed weight is reallocated to Factor 3, which is the channel through which dollar conditions actually reach this pair.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Dollar funding conditions are benign and abundant, and for this cross that cuts both ways almost exactly. SOFR printed 3.65-3.68% against IORB of 3.65%, an effectively zero spread; standing repo facility usage was nil through August; and QT formally ended on 1 December 2025 with the Desk now buying Treasury bills to maintain ample reserves. Cheap and abundant dollars are the precondition for a carry trade to keep funding itself, a positive for the pair through the same channel as Factor 3. Working the other way, the Fed is priced 57-66% to hike on 16 September, and a firmer dollar hits a high-beta base currency with a 3.6%-of-GDP external deficit and no Fed swap line harder than it hits the funding currency. Both dossiers score their own USD funding factor as Bearish for their own currency at almost identical confidence — New Zealand 55, Japan 58 — so the bilateral netting is plus 3, inside the noise.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the dollar channel remains close to neutral for the cross and confidence falls two points because two identified structural forces point in opposite directions with roughly equal weight. On one side, the Fed hiking into an expanding balance sheet is the classic right-hand-side-of-the-smile configuration, hurting the base leg more than the quote leg given lower liquidity and the absent Fed swap line. On the other side, the quote dossier identifies two named channels that would make the yen leg of the basis a yen-positive force: Japan's USD 550bn US investment commitment pushing the dollar-yen basis more negative through receiving flows, and life-insurer hedge-ratio normalisation creating widening pressure on the short-term basis with simultaneous spot yen demand. Neither can be sized because no quoted cross-currency basis level is obtainable for either leg, the largest unresolved input in this factor.

Conviction is 3 because the two heaviest factors agree and the resolving event is dated and close, but not 4 because a 150 to 175bp carry in a 14-VIX world is a real cost of being short and because the risk factor would reverse the score if the volatility regime simply persists. strategic.score_interpretation: A net score of minus 0.3393 is well beyond the minus 0.10 threshold and is a materially stronger Bearish reading than the tactical minus 0.1885, meaning the expectation is for NZD/JPY to FALL over one to six months. Six factors are Bearish and carry 0.56 of the applied weight, contributing minus 0.3764 between them; the distribution is broad, with Policy and Rates, Guidance and Credibility, and Inflation and Growth the three largest. Only one factor is Bullish — Fiscal and Sovereign Risk at plus 0.0371. Three factors are Neutral and carry 0.27 of the weight, and one of them, External Balance at a 0.16 weight, contributes exactly nothing because both economies are being hit by the same energy and commodity shock from opposite sides of an identical trade. This is genuinely a breadth-and-depth result: the heaviest factor and the third-heaviest both point the same way, and four lighter factors agree.
strategic.rationale: At strategic weights the case against the pair broadens from two factors to six and the score roughly doubles, which is unusual and worth being explicit about. The dominant mechanism is differential compression. From 175bp after the 2 September hike, the RBNZ's own republished track allows for roughly one further quarter-point move to 3.00%, and the base dossier's strategic view is that the cycle stops there and the 9 December track is revised down. The Bank of Japan is on the opposite trajectory, with 35 of 54 economists expecting at least 1.50% by end-March 2027 and half of a separate panel naming 1.75% as terminal, so the gap narrows toward 125bp by the 18 December meeting and 100-125bp thereafter. Guidance reinforces it with dated precision: the BoJ publishes its Outlook Report on 30 October, two days after the RBNZ's Monetary Policy Review on 28 October, and the July edition had already revised FY2027 core CPI up to 2.4% while reframing the objective toward preventing an upward deviation — a change of reaction function that converts every upside surprise into tightening. Inflation and growth reinforce it again, because the two CPI paths cross inside the window: New Zealand's petrol base effect unwinds at the September-quarter print in October while Japan's energy-subsidy suppression of roughly 40-50bp unwinds in the other direction. The conflict in the dossiers is genuine and is scored honestly: Japan's external accounts are deteriorating faster than New Zealand's, and the framework's own commodity direction rules make oil and LNG a strong yen negative that New Zealand shares only partially, which is exactly why a 0.16-weight factor contributes zero rather than the large negative that a naive current-account comparison would give. Japan's fiscal position is the single Bullish contributor and it is not trivial: a JPY 36.6trn debt-service line at a 3.8% assumed rate means each further 100bp of BoJ tightening costs about 0.9% of GDP, and an inverted 25s30s says the long end is pricing supply rather than policy. What is priced is a mechanical forward discount of roughly 1.9% annualised, which is arithmetic; what is not priced is a BoJ terminal above 1.50%, an RBNZ track revised down on 9 December, or a Japanese life-insurer hedge-ratio normalisation that would put sustained spot yen demand into a cross with no depth. The path of least resistance is a contested grind lower with the decisive dates being the 30 October BoJ Outlook, the New Zealand election in November and the 9 December RBNZ Monetary Policy Statement. Conviction is 3 rather than 4 because the carry cost of 150-175bp is real, because the modal risk-regime path remains carry-friendly, and because the heaviest bullish offset — Japan's fiscal arithmetic — would strengthen precisely as the BoJ delivers the tightening the bearish case depends on.
strategic.g10_relative_ranking: Strategically NZD/JPY is one of the more attractive yen-long expressions in the G10, ranking ahead of AUD/JPY on a risk-adjusted basis because it costs 150-175bp of carry rather than 335bp for the same directional exposure, and ahead of CAD/JPY where the policy comparison is flat and the oil leg cuts against the trade. It ranks behind short CHF/JPY, the only long-yen expression in the G10 that is paid to wait at plus 100bp of policy carry, and behind short GBP/JPY on pure fundamental spread. Among New Zealand dollar crosses it ranks second behind long AUD/NZD, which expresses the same New Zealand policy and external thesis while earning 185bp of carry rather than paying 150-175, at the lowest realised volatility in the complex — but NZD/JPY is the cleaner expression for anyone who also wants the Bank of Japan normalisation leg, which AUD/NZD does not contain.

consensus_divergence.why_we_differ: No major bank publishes a standing NZD/JPY forecast that could be located from a nameable research venue, so there is no bank consensus for this pair to differ from. What exists is (a) algorithmic extrapolation services calibrated before the 2-3 September break, and (b) cross-derived arithmetic multiplying two independent bank consensuses for NZD/USD and USD/JPY, which multiplies rather than averages forecast errors. Three bilateral factors are weighed differently by us: Guidance and Credibility at a 0.12 strategic weight, where the cross-derived arithmetic prices the RBNZ track at face value and the BoJ's at a discount when the BoJ has said in writing its pace will be faster than market expectations; the NZD/USD leg of the arithmetic embeds a hawkish RBNZ path that 2 September did not deliver; and almost none of the reference set is conditioned on a Bank of Japan that might abandon its twice-yearly tightening rhythm.
consensus_divergence.payoff_if_right: The differential falls from 175bp to 125bp or less, a 29% reduction in the only thing paying the holder of the long side, at the same moment the fundamental case for holding it deteriorates on the inflation and guidance channels — worth 284 pips on spot in the base case and 544 in the tail, against 88 pips of carry cost.
consensus_divergence.risk_if_wrong: The narrow way is that the RBNZ over-delivers relative to its own track while the BoJ pauses, holding the differential at 175bp and leaving a short paying carry for nothing; the broad way is that the risk regime simply persists, in which case Factor 3 alone flips the tactical score positive and NZD/JPY keeps working as the base currency's one working carry expression. The broad scenario is the one in which we are wrong slowly and expensively, which is why conviction is 3 at both horizons rather than 4.

cross_horizon_consistency.explanation: The horizons agree in direction and differ substantially in magnitude, with the strategic score roughly 1.8 times the tactical, almost entirely a weight-and-breadth effect. Tactically the case rests on two factors — Policy and Rates and Inflation and Growth — partly offset by a Bullish Risk Appetite factor. External Balance at a 0.16 strategic weight contributes zero at both horizons because the two economies are absorbing the same commodity shock from opposite ends of an identical trade.
cross_horizon_consistency.trading_implication: Run the tactical and strategic expressions as one position with two tranches rather than two positions — establish half into the September cluster with a 93.75 daily-close stop, and add the second half only on a confirmed weekly close below 90.925 or on a November retracement into the falling 200-day, which keeps the average entry above spot and defers 40-50 pips of carry cost to the phase in which the thesis actually resolves.

catalysts.rationale: The only G10 guidance event publishing a numeric policy path. The Committee raised the OCR unanimously to 2.75% but the new track indicated only the chance of one further quarter-point hike before year-end and was characterised locally as more dovish than anticipated against expectations of a peak nearer 3.28-3.50%. The Bank also conceded that annual inflation excluding vehicle fuels was 2.9%, inside the band. The pair fell 1.51 yen on the day and a further 1.23 yen the next session.

catalysts.rationale: The first preliminary showed +0.3% q/q with capex at -1.2%, but the MoF corporate survey showed Q2 capex up 1.6% y/y against a 0.2% consensus, skewing the revision higher and supporting the BoJ path. The same release carries the July current account after June's first monthly deficit in seventeen months. The two halves cut opposite ways: a stronger GDP revision is bearish NZD/JPY through the policy channel, a second current-account deficit bullish through the external channel.

Dairy is roughly 30% of New Zealand merchandise exports and GDT is the highest-frequency commodity event affecting either leg. Event 411 was the fourth consecutive positive auction at +0.9%, but whole milk powder was down 0.1% at USD 3,585/t and remains below its 2 June level, with the ANZ dairy sub-index down 11.3% y/y. catalysts.event: Federal Open Market Committee decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.rationale: No dollar leg exists in this cross, so the FOMC reaches it through two channels that point opposite ways. A hike, priced at 57-66%, firms the dollar on the right-hand side of the smile and hits the high-beta base currency harder than the funding currency; but a hawkish Fed that sustains the equity and credit rally directly supports the carry trade. The base leg is the more exposed because the RBNZ has no standing Fed swap line and New Zealand funds a 3.6%-of-GDP external deficit continuously.

catalysts.event: New Zealand Q2 GDP and Japan August national CPI, same-day collision
catalysts.rationale: The highest-information bilateral data event in the tactical window, because both legs print first-tier data in the same session. New Zealand grew 0.8% in the March quarter with surveys pointing higher but retail volumes negative and unemployment at a decade-high 5.6%. Japanese national core printed 1.8% in July with the BoJ's ex-special-factors measure at 2.3%, Tokyo core accelerating three months running, and an energy subsidy suppressing the headline by 40-50bp. A Japanese core print at or above 2.0% alongside a soft New Zealand GDP figure reprices both front ends against the pair in one session.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting decision
catalysts.rationale: The largest single event in the tactical window and the only live catalyst left after the RBNZ resolved. Roughly 80-90% of a 25bp move to 1.25% is priced, so the decision is not the trade — the press conference is, because cumulative pricing implies only about 1.21% after 18 December against an economist terminal centred on 1.75%. Every 25bp delivered cuts the pair's carry by a sixth. The risk has since skewed further with hawkish comments from Governor Ueda and board member Takata raising the possibility of an outsized rate increase.

catalysts.event: New Zealand Treasury Pre-election Economic and Fiscal Update (PREFU 2026)
catalysts.rationale: An independent Treasury view published into an election campaign, against a Budget 2026 path with net core Crown debt rising from 41.9% of GDP in FY25 to a peak of 46.1% in FY28 and the return to surplus placed in FY29, in front of two of three agencies already on negative outlook. The transmission is a headline risk premium on the base leg in a currency with 88,964 contracts of futures open interest and no domestic buyer of scale, against a quote currency no agency has moved off stable outlook in 2026.

catalysts.event: US FY2027 appropriations deadline and Japanese interim fiscal half-year end
catalysts.rationale: Two coincident events pointing the same way for this cross. A US shutdown is precedented — two occurred in 2026 — and would be risk-negative, hitting the highest-beta cross in the G10 through the base leg while bidding the funding leg. Separately, the Japanese interim book-closing generates documented repatriation and dividend-related yen demand. The pair's own term structure carries no premium for either.

catalysts.event: Statistics New Zealand Consumers Price Index, September 2026 quarter
catalysts.rationale: The inflection print for the base leg's policy path. Petrol contributed 27.5% of the annual rise to 4.1% and Brent has fallen roughly 12% from its July high, while the RBNZ's July review already cut the September-quarter peak to 3.3% from the May track's 4.3%. A print at or below 3.5% with the sectoral factor model at or below 2.7% removes the justification for anything beyond the one further hike the 2 September track allows, one week before the 28 October Review. Japan's CPI moves the opposite way over the same window.

catalysts.event: Reserve Bank of New Zealand OCR decision with Monetary Policy Review
catalysts.rationale: No new track is published at a Review, so the content is framing rather than projection. It is the Bank's first opportunity to soften the 2 September framing and falls the week after the September-quarter CPI. The July Review demonstrated the Bank will revise its near-term inflation path between statements, having cut the September-quarter CPI peak from 4.3% to 3.3% inside eight weeks.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting with quarterly Outlook Report
catalysts.rationale: The projection round on the quote leg, falling two days after the RBNZ Review in the tightest guidance collision on the calendar. The July Outlook had already revised FY2027 core CPI up to 2.4%, described CPI risks as skewed to the upside and reframed the objective to preventing an upward deviation. The October revision incorporates the energy-subsidy unwind, a terms-of-trade shock and a yen weaker than the JPY 152.57 corporate planning rate. Outlook revisions are consistently under-anticipated and this one has an upward skew.

catalysts.event: Statistics New Zealand Labour Market Statistics, September 2026 quarter
catalysts.rationale: Unemployment reached 5.6% in the June quarter, the highest since September 2015, with RBNZ survey respondents expecting 5.24% one year ahead and private-sector ordinary-time wage growth of 2.0% against 4.1% inflation meaning real wages are falling 2.1%. The bilateral contrast is stark: Japanese unemployment is 2.4% with real wages positive for six consecutive months on a 5.01% shunto. A further rise would be hard to reconcile with even the one hike the September track allows.

A three-year parliamentary cycle in which the parties differ materially on housing, immigration and fiscal policy, all of which transmit directly to the currency of a 5.3 million-person open economy. The bilateral asymmetry is that Japan has no scheduled national election inside the horizon after February 2026's supermajority, so the political-risk premium accrues entirely to the base leg — and the pair's six-month implied volatility of 7.91% carries no premium for it.

catalysts.event: Reserve Bank of New Zealand OCR decision with Monetary Policy Statement and new OCR track
catalysts.rationale: The decisive event for the strategic thesis and the second track republication inside the horizon. By December the Bank will have seen the September-quarter CPI with the fuel base effect unwinding, labour data and two further GDP prints. The strategic case requires a track revised down from the 2 September version, which already allows only one further hike; this is where Guidance and Credibility turns decisively against the base leg.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting decision
catalysts.rationale: The largest identified gap between guidance and pricing in either dossier. Cumulative OIS implies a policy rate of only about 1.21% after this meeting, so a second 2026 hike is barely priced, while half of 36 surveyed economists name 1.75% as terminal and 35 of 54 expect at least 1.50% by end-March 2027. A December move would be a repricing rather than a confirmation, cutting the cross's carry to roughly 125bp nine days after the RBNZ is expected to have revised its own track down.

catalysts.event: Japan FY2027 draft budget Cabinet approval
catalysts.rationale: The one dated catalyst inside the horizon that favours the pair. Ministry requests total approximately JPY 143trn with a record JPY 36.6trn debt-service line at a 3.8% assumed rate, against a stated new-issuance cap of roughly JPY 40trn versus JPY 29.6trn in the FY2026 initial budget. If the cap is breached and the 30-year JGB moves above 4.50%, the yield rise becomes unambiguously a fiscal risk premium with no currency-positive content, and the yen leg of the bearish case weakens materially.

assumptions: Price payload metadata: dataPoints 130, dateRange 2026-03-06 to 2026-09-03, spot 91.63785 at spotDate 2026-09-03, computationRange 2008-01-14 to 2026-09-03 (4863 weekday bars), pipSize 0.01, weekendBarsDropped 0. Moving averages, support/resistance zones, 52-week range percentiles and 200-week figures are computed over the whole stored history per computationRange, not over the 130 bars shown; the 130 bars are used only for the recent price-action narrative and the higher-high/lower-low structure. All moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes on a weekday-only series; realised volatility is annualised on 252 trading days.

The spot date (2026-09-03) postdates the valuation date (2026-09-01) by two sessions and this is material: the payload spot of 91.63785 is a close struck one session after the 2 September RBNZ decision and encompasses two sessions in which the pair fell 2.74 yen (2.90%). Every level, target, pip calculation, percentage move and distance-to-average is anchored to 91.63785, and no fresher web quote has been substituted. The entry framework prioritises retracements over market execution for this reason.

This is pass 2 of 2. Every factor stance, confidence, evidence_type, applied weight, weighted contribution, net score, conviction and rationale is carried through unchanged from the first pass, which scored them without the price payload. Nothing has been re-scored because the chart agrees or disagrees; where price data or post-scoring research materially changes the picture (Factor 3, Factor 6, Factor 9), that is stated in clearly labelled report notes and addenda that leave the scored numbers untouched.

Implied volatility is an estimate and a floor, not a quote. NZD/JPY has no listed option, so the payload constructs the surface from the variance identity using a realised correlation of 0.533 in place of an unobservable implied one; the substitution understated direct Eurex quotes by 8.7% to 17.8% in tested cases and by a 14.4% median across seventeen pairs. The 7.692% 3-month figure is measured at 94.7 days, not 90, and is treated as a floor throughout (corrected range 8.3-9.1%).

No skew data exists for this cross. No NZD/JPY 25-delta risk reversal, vol skew or barrier level is obtainable from any free citable source. Where skew is discussed it is by explicit reference to other pairs (USD/JPY, EUR/JPY, EUR/USD) used only to establish that yen-upside strikes are richly bid across the complex; no NZD/JPY skew value is asserted anywhere in this report.

Forwards are derived, not quoted. The forward points and outrights are constructed by applying the payload's futures-implied roll premium of -192.7bp annualised (6J/6N calendar spread, observed 2026-08-31) to the payload spot on an actual/365 basis. They are model forwards from a cached futures observation, not dealer quotes. By covered interest parity the premium is the interest differential plus the cross-currency basis, which cannot be separated without an OIS curve; no quoted cross-currency basis level for NZD/JPY, USD/JPY or NZD/USD is obtainable from any free source.

Rates block staleness: the 10-year differential of +1.79pp rests on cached monthly IRLTLT01 observations dated 2026-06-01, roughly 92 days stale at the valuation date. Where live legs are discussed (NZ 4.74%, JGB 10-year 3.00% on 1 September), the resulting ~174bp is presented as a mixed-basis approximation and flagged, never blended with the cached figure. The base policy rate of 2.50% is dated 2026-08-28 and has since been raised to 2.75%; both the 150bp and 175bp post-hike differentials are stated at every point of use.

Bilateral trade is used as supplied. The IMF DOTS block (2024) is used directly in Factor 5 and was not re-estimated from the web; it is two years old and used only to establish that the direct trade relationship is immaterial to the cross, a conclusion robust to the staleness.

Web research scope: five searches were conducted, restricted to what neither dossier nor the price payload captures — pair-specific forecast venues, named chart patterns and pattern-derived levels, pair-specific positioning and flow dynamics including Japanese retail and Uridashi channels, and post-2 September event interpretation. Support and resistance levels were NOT web-searched: every zone comes from the payload's computed zones with its own touch count. Web-sourced pattern levels (55-day EMA, 94.21 resistance, 91.02 support, 89.44 Fibonacci) are presented as corroborating context alongside the computed zones, not mixed into the ranked list.

Consensus is absent rather than adverse. No bank publishes a standing NZD/JPY forecast locatable from a nameable research venue. The reference set is explicitly named as (a) algorithmic extrapolation services and (b) cross-derived arithmetic from the two legs' separate bank consensuses, and combining two independent forecast distributions multiplies rather than averages their errors.

Inherited dossier flags propagate unaltered and are not re-verified here: BIS REER figures are cache-sourced with no fetchable BIS page and disagree with a direct pull; New Zealand CFTC positioning figures conflict between the Traders in Financial Futures and legacy non-commercial series; the Federal Reserve September hike probability spans 26-66% across sources; Japanese IMF debt/deficit figures and all sovereign ratings are uncited; the operative US tariff on Japanese motor vehicles could not be established; and the JPY dossier's own spot anchor of 160.115 is a store close vendor sources do not corroborate.
Weights: five adjustments were made from defaults across the two horizons, each within the ±0.05 limit and each with a stated bilateral reason; both adjusted sets sum to exactly 1.00.

Net stances were derived, not chosen: -0.1885 and -0.3393 both sit beyond the -0.10 threshold and are therefore both Bearish, applied mechanically. Conviction of 3 at each horizon is the separate judgement about how much weight to place behind a direction the arithmetic has already fixed.
